lesson.title: Reassembly: Putting Fragmented Packets Back Together
lesson.summary: Reassembly is the process, carried out only at the final destination host, of collecting every fragment of a split packet and reconstructing its original payload using each fragment's offset and the more fragments flag.
lesson.body:
Fragmentation splits an oversized packet into pieces that fit across a constrained link, but those pieces are not useful to anything above the network layer until they are put back together into the packet they originally were. That reconstruction is called reassembly, and it happens at exactly one place: the final destination host. Intermediate routers that fragmented a packet, or simply forwarded fragments they did not create, never try to reassemble anything themselves, since reassembly requires holding onto every fragment until the full set has arrived, and routers are built to move packets along quickly rather than buffer them.

The destination host groups incoming fragments using the same Identification field, together with the source address, destination address, and protocol, that fragmentation stamped onto every piece of the same original packet. As fragments trickle in, possibly out of order since different fragments can take different paths through the network, the host uses each one's Fragment Offset to place its payload at the correct position within a reassembly buffer. The fragment whose More Fragments flag is set to zero tells the host the total size of the original payload, since that fragment's offset plus its own length marks the very end of the data. Once every byte position from the start of the payload through that final marked end has actually been filled in by an arrived fragment, reassembly is complete, and the host hands the reconstructed, original packet up to the transport layer protocol, TCP or UDP, exactly as if it had never been split at all.

Continuing the three fragment example from the previous chapter, imagine the destination receives fragment three first, with offset 370 and More Fragments set to zero. From this alone, the host already knows the total payload is 2960 bytes, from the offset, plus 1020 bytes, the length of this final fragment, for 3980 bytes altogether, even though it has not seen the beginning of the data yet. It places those 1020 bytes at the correct position in its buffer and waits. Fragment one, offset 0, arrives next and fills in the start of the buffer. Only once fragment two, offset 185, finally arrives and fills the remaining gap in the middle does the buffer become complete, at which point the host reassembles the full 3980 byte payload and passes it upward.

Reassembly is not free, and this is part of why fragmentation is generally avoided when possible. A destination host has to hold onto partial fragment sets in memory and run a timer against them, because if even one fragment out of a set is lost in transit, nothing about IP allows the host to ask for just that missing piece to be resent, unlike a lost segment in a reliable transport protocol. If the timer expires before every fragment has arrived, the host discards the entire partial set and, for IPv4, can send back an ICMP time exceeded message with a code specifically meaning fragment reassembly time exceeded. This all-or-nothing cost is a major reason many modern systems try to avoid fragmentation altogether, for instance by discovering a path's smallest MTU in advance and sizing packets to fit it from the start, rather than relying on fragmentation and reassembly to clean up afterward.
